27940:
Concluding a series on the attributes of God, this sermon from Exodus 34:14, "the Lord, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God", presents divine jealousy as the motivation believers need to resist the pull of a prosperous, distracting world. Unlike sinful jealousy, rooted in self and insecurity, God's jealousy is a holy zeal to protect what is rightly his and to keep an exclusive relationship, a consuming fire against all who dishonour him. First, God is jealous for his own glory. Creation, the image of God in humanity and redemption itself exist for his praise, and the first commandments forbid every rival god because he is jealous.

Second, God is jealous for his Son. The Father's zeal will establish Christ's endless kingdom and has placed all things under his feet, which is why salvation is found in no other name: Jesus alone will be honoured forever as Redeemer. Third, God is jealous for his people, as a faithful husband for his bride. His jealousy is loving, faithful in protecting his elect and holy in giving himself wholly to them, so he rightly calls for undivided devotion and grieves when they seek satisfaction in broken cisterns (Jeremiah 2). Believers are urged to confess their idols, thank Christ for bearing their unfaithfulness, follow him wholeheartedly, and ask not only whether something is sinful but whether it increases their delight in God.
27941:
Closing a series on the growing Christian, this sermon on Philippians 3:20-21 asks what drives believers to live faithfully in a world full of trials, temptation and sorrow, and answers with the Christian hope. First, the position of that hope: our citizenship is in heaven. Unlike the enemies of the cross who live for this world, believers are pilgrims bound for a better country prepared by God. Christians are urged not to be attached to or attracted by the world, despite pressure even from professing believers. Their citizenship can never be revoked by sickness, sorrow or sin, so they should store up treasure in heaven.

Second, the person of that hope: we eagerly wait for a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ. He came first as a humble servant but will return as a glorious King to consummate his marriage with his bride. Believers should long for him as a child waits for a parent or a bride for her groom, rather than for possessions, while unbelievers will dread his coming as Judge. Third, the possession of that hope: a new body. Christ will transform our weak, decaying bodies to be like his glorious body by the same power with which he subjects all things to himself, so we can stand in God's presence (1 Corinthians 15). Listeners are asked to examine their relationship with Christ and bear good fruit.
28901:
Preaching from Philippians 1:20-26, written while Paul awaited a verdict that could mean death, this sermon sets out basic Christianity: Christ is the purpose-driven life. Many professing believers live for their children, careers or comfort, treating Jesus as a slogan on a t-shirt or bumper sticker, but the new birth makes a person new, with affections that show in how they live. First, believers live for Christ. "For to me, to live is Christ" means an active life devoted to exalting him, not a part-time faith. As Romans 14:7-8 shows, this applies to every Christian, not to Paul alone.

Second, believers long for Christ. Paul was hard pressed between fruitful labour and the far better gain of being with Christ. The word "depart" pictures a prisoner unchained, a camp packed up and a ship untied from the dock: life on earth is a brief stopover before sailing into Christ's presence, so death is promotion, not demotion. Third, believers linger for the sake of Christ's body. Paul was convinced he would remain for the church's progress and joy in the faith, and every believer is likewise called to bear fruit by serving the brethren sacrificially. Listeners are urged to repent and board the ship by faith, and to remind struggling believers that they are only docked here for a little while.
28981:
In this second sermon on gossip, the church is presented as Christ's beloved bride and body, so slandering a fellow believer is like throwing mud at his fiancée or wounding his body. The sermon first answers three common excuses. Sharing a burden about someone who offended you is not what Scripture means: Colossians 3:12-13 calls believers to bear with and forgive one another. Venting to a spouse is still slander, which 1 Peter 2:1 says must be put away. Leaving out names still defiles the hearer and cannot edify (Ephesians 4:29). Believers must instead protect Christ's bride, covering a brother's shame as Christ covered theirs.

Four commands follow. Do not broadcast gossip, for without wood the fire goes out (Proverbs 26:20). Do not listen to it: gossip tastes like dainty morsels because it feeds self-righteousness, the desire for control and the wish to be accepted, so cut it off and find satisfaction in Christ. Separate yourself from those with a pattern of divisive talk (Titus 3:10). Leaders are not exempt: they must refuse venting sessions, help those genuinely seeking counsel, hear both sides and establish facts only by two or three witnesses. Finally, those tempted to vent should go to the brother directly, pray for him, dwell on what is good in him and seek fellowship with him, so the church is known as gospel people, not gossips.
28983:
In this first of two topical messages on gossip, the church is thanked for the Christ-centred, blood-bought unity God has given it, seen in the way members care for one another, and is warned to guard it. Alongside false teaching, gossip is one of the two sins most destructive to a local church. Slander spreads false, malicious information, while gossip spreads harmful information whether true or not. Both aim to drag a brother's name through the mud so that the gossip looks good. Scripture uses the two words almost interchangeably, and the sermon shows that gossip destroys three parties.

First, it destroys the slanderer. Proverbs calls such a person senseless and worthless, and Leviticus 19:16 places slander beside acting against a neighbour's life, treating it as a kind of murder; spreading strife among brothers is listed among the things the Lord hates most. Second, it destroys the hearer. Gossip separates intimate friends, often arriving subtly as a burden to pray about or a tearful victim story, and whoever listens without defending a brother's honour becomes an evildoer and a liar. Third, it destroys the offended brother, condemned behind his back with no chance to answer, so that trust turns to ashes. The Greek word for slanderer also names the devil, while Christ covers his people's sin. Unbelievers are told they need new life in Christ, not mere moral reform.
28999:
Preaching on Mark 12:32-34, where Jesus tells a scribe, "You are not far from the kingdom of God", this sermon warns that being near the kingdom is not the same as being in it. Nothing matters more than entering God's everlasting kingdom, yet many are self-deceived, believing they are inside when they are only at the gate. First, the scribe was not far. He was committed to the truth, openly agreeing with Jesus instead of walking away like other religious leaders, and seekers of truth are seeking Christ, who is the truth. He also understood the right priority: loving God with all one's being and one's neighbour as oneself matters more than all burnt offerings and outward ritual.

Second, he was not safe. Like a man an inch from Noah's ark or Lot's wife looking back, those who come close yet never enter are completely lost, and their consciences will torment them with regret. Third, he was not in. His response was purely intellectual: he agreed with the law but never asked whether he had kept it, what he must do to be saved, or whether Jesus, standing before him, would save him. Christ was born under the law to redeem those condemned by it. Listeners are pleaded with to let the law break them and to come all the way to Christ, who casts out none who come.
29086:
Focusing on a single verse, Mark 10:31, "many who are first will be last, and the last first", this sermon begins with the life of Jesus himself: born in a stable, poor, rejected and crucified, last by every worldly measure, yet exalted by God above every name. His life is both our motive and our pattern, so those counted last for his sake are not losers, for they will be first. Read in context after Peter's words, "we have left everything and followed you", the verse also carries three warnings. First, it warns the rich young ruler and all unbelievers who love their wealth. Such people rarely admit it, but they spend their lives expanding earthly kingdoms and turn from Christ when he calls; on the day of great reversal their riches will be worthless.

Second, it warns Judas and every false convert. Judas came closest to the kingdom yet was lost, and Bible reading, sound preaching, godly family, ministry and gifts are no proof of salvation without wholehearted surrender to Christ. Third, it warns Peter and lukewarm believers whose motives drift. What matters is not only what we do for Christ but whom we do it for, and 1 Corinthians 3 teaches that eternal rewards depend on this. Believers are urged to give themselves away for Jesus' sake and invest in eternity, and unbelievers to come wholly to Christ.
29226:
Preaching on the feeding of the four thousand in Mark 8:1-10, this sermon warns that biblical orthodoxy without compassion is among the ugliest things in the world, because it paints a false portrait of Christ, whose every word and miracle was coloured by compassion. Only here does Jesus say in his own words, "I have compassion on the crowd." He shows it in three ways. First, he cares for the needy. After three days of teaching a mostly Gentile crowd, he cared not only for their souls but for their empty stomachs, so believers can cast every anxiety on him, physical and spiritual.

Second, he caters for the needy. The disciples questioned how so many could be fed, revealing not doubt about his power but their lack of compassion for Gentiles, whom Jews despised as unclean. Jesus took everything they had, seven loaves and a few fish, and made them waiters serving those they looked down on, teaching them heavenly compassion without partiality before they carried the gospel to the world. Third, he completes all that the needy lack. The crowd did not merely eat; they were satisfied, with seven baskets left over, pointing to Christ himself as the bread of life who satisfies the hungry soul. Believers are urged to model his compassion by caring practically for the needy in the church, not just proclaiming truth.
29228:
Preaching through Mark 7:31-37, this sermon asks what it looks like to be truly satisfied in Jesus, the bread of life. Those who delight in him love him, and that love leads them to model his life before others. First, they model his purpose. Jesus walked some 400 kilometres through Gentile regions to seek and save the lost. The people of the Decapolis, who once begged him to leave, now brought a deaf man and begged him to help, because the healed demoniac had told everyone what the Lord had done. Christ's purpose is contagious: those who love him love what he loves, and they bring their health, wealth, time and energy under that purpose.

Second, they model his affection. Jesus took the man aside privately, put his fingers into his ears, touched his tongue and sighed toward heaven, showing that he understood and felt his suffering. His healing was born of compassion, not mere duty. Third, they model his gospel. Jesus silenced talk of mere physical healing because the saving message is the cross: Christ bore God's wrath for sinners and rose to grant forgiveness to all who believe. Applications include speaking the truth in love and wives winning unbelieving husbands through visibly gentle submission. Those who do not model Christ are urged to examine their salvation and come to him.
29449:
In this second sermon on Judas Iscariot, the apostle stands as a warning to everyone who is in the church but not in Christ. Like a police officer trusting a paper "bulletproof vest", false converts trust Bible reading, prayer, church attendance or ministry rather than the bleeding Lamb of God. First, the danger of being a false convert. At the Last Supper Jesus declared that his death was God's ordained plan, yet Judas remained fully responsible: "it would have been better for that man if he had not been born" (Mark 14:21). As Matthew 10 shows, those who hear the gospel and reject it face a judgment more severe than Sodom's.

Second, the reasons for that danger. Externally, rejecting the blood-bought invitation tramples the Son of God underfoot and outrages the Spirit of grace (Hebrews 10:29). Internally, conscience will torment the lost forever with regret over every warning ignored. Third, 1 John supplies biblical tests of genuine faith. Is God himself exposing the sin in your heart? Does love for him produce obedience? Does his love lead you to hate worldly cravings? Does love for God overflow in love for his children? These tests do not save, but they show whether faith is real. Those who are unconverted are urged to come wholly to the crucified and risen Christ, whose remedy is only an inch away.
29450:
Concluding the series on the twelve apostles, this first of two sermons on Judas Iscariot (Mark 3:19) presents him not as an encouragement but as a warning: not everyone who calls himself a Christian truly is one. Chosen by Jesus as an apostle, Judas was nonetheless called a devil and the son of destruction. He had the right facts about Christ, and perhaps even feelings for him, but never true faith that surrendered his life to Christ's lordship. First, Judas, like most false converts, was almost saved yet entirely lost. For more than two years he heard Jesus preach, saw his miracles and watched others rejoice in forgiveness, yet he let go of the rope just short of the shore.

Second, Judas was extremely subtle. He blended in so well that the other apostles made him their treasurer, and he disguised his thievery as concern for the poor when Mary anointed Jesus (John 12). At the Last Supper each disciple asked "Is it I?" before suspecting him. Third, the sermon exposes unbiblical grounds of assurance: Bible reading, sound preaching, godly family, ministry roles, spiritual gifts, a sinner's prayer or baptism. Judas had more of these than anyone yet was lost. Listeners are urged to examine themselves, come wholly to Christ, and praise the grace that saved them.
29546:
Continuing through Colossians, this sermon turns from the negative commands to the positive virtues of Colossians 3:12, beginning with the little word "so". Because believers have put on the new self and Christ is all and in all, they are to display Christ's character. The sermon warns against "Christless virtues": being nice or moral apart from Jesus breeds either shallow self-righteousness or exhausting, joyless striving. Instead, believers are reminded that they are chosen of God, holy and beloved, so his love moves them to worship and to make their lives a display of Christ to his people.

Paul then calls them to put on four garments, each learned by gazing at Christ. Compassion is suffering with the hurting, as Jesus wept at Lazarus' tomb and touched the leper. Kindness is extending a helping hand without expecting a return, as Christ's yoke is kind and he embraces sinners however filthy. Humility is lowliness of mind: neither false humility nor boasting, but esteeming others above oneself, as the glorious Lord became a servant and bore our sin. Gentleness is power under control, the willingness to suffer injury rather than inflict it, seen as Jesus went silently to the cross praying for his enemies. Unbelievers are pleaded with to come to such a gentle and gracious Saviour.
29786:
Beginning with the story of a young man sinking in quicksand, this sermon asks how believers can find true rest and renew their hearts when trials, illness or besetting sin seem to pull them under. The answer is found in Isaiah 42:16, from the "book of consolation", where God declares five times what he will do: lead the blind, guide them, turn darkness into light, smooth rugged places and not leave them undone. First, the sovereignty of God. Isaiah's precise prophecies of judgment by Assyria and Babylon, and of Cyrus decades before his birth, show that God is the author of history. They comforted the exiles and point to the Messiah who will return to reign, so believers can rest in his righteous right hand.

Second, the power of God. The blind who did not know the way describes every believer before conversion, like a man at a Japanese shrine drawing curse after curse. Regenerating a depraved heart displays God's power even more than creating the universe, and that same power upholds his people. Third, the remembrance of God. Because his people are prone to forget him (Deuteronomy 6:12), believers must deliberately remember the Lord in prosperity, in adversity and in despair, making Christ their one pursuit as Paul did. Even a faith hanging by a thread is held because Christ spun it. Unbelievers are urged to repent and believe.
29800:
Working through Luke 1:18-25, this sermon examines what happens when unbelief collides with God's promises. What keeps a sinner from Christ is not the size of his sin but unbelief, for one cry of faith is enough. Even for believers, doubting God's word insults his character and invites his fatherly discipline. First, unbelief questions God's integrity. Zechariah, a righteous priest standing in the holy place before an angel, measured God's promise of a son against his own age and his wife's barrenness, though he knew how God had opened the wombs of Sarah, Rebekah, Rachel and Hannah. Believers do the same when they give up praying for an unsaved relative or accept defeat by a besetting sin, making Christ look small and their problems large.

Second, unbelief brings God's discipline. Gabriel, whose name proclaims God's might, struck Zechariah mute and deaf until the promise was fulfilled, removing him from his ministry. This was not punishment for sin, which Christ bore, but the correction of a loving Father. Third, unbelief cannot stop God's grace. Elizabeth conceived, and while her doubting husband was silent she praised the Lord for taking away her disgrace. Christians are urged to confess their unbelief, believe what God has said and follow Elizabeth's example rather than Zechariah's.
30019:
Opening a three-part study of Job under the theme "the sovereign Lord, the suffering saint and the devil's role", this sermon looks at Job 1:1-5 to present a Christian character worth imitating, because understanding Job's character is the key to understanding his suffering. God himself says there is none like Job on the earth: blameless and upright, fearing God and turning away from evil. Blameless does not mean sinless but growing in holiness, hating sin and putting it to death, with inner holiness visible in outward conduct. The sermon warns believers not to assume, as Job's friends did, that every suffering saint must be sinning, since God sometimes allows suffering for his own glory, as Jesus showed in John 9.

Job was also generous in heart. Though he was the greatest man in the East, his wealth did not lead him astray; he provided for his many servants and their families, and when everything was taken he still worshipped, saying, "The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away." He was spiritual in heart, rising early to offer sacrifices in case his children had sinned against God in their hearts. Fathers are urged to pray for their children and feed them spiritually rather than only providing material things, and believers to love and pray for their church family, so that they stand firm when trials come.
30119:
Preaching on Luke 6:1-5, where the disciples pick and eat grain on the Sabbath, this sermon exposes legalism: piling man-made rules on top of God's commands until no one can breathe beneath them. Self-righteous people love legalism because it lets them polish their own goodness and condemn others. First, legalism condemns. What the disciples did was permitted by Deuteronomy 23:25, yet the Pharisees, acting as self-appointed referees, accused them of breaking their own rules. Their traditions had turned the Sabbath, God's gift of rest and delight, into a burden, like fences built around a garden until no one can enjoy it. Believers are warned not to confuse their own interpretation of God's law with God's law itself.

Second, Jesus defends. He answers from Scripture, pointing to David eating the consecrated bread: if God in compassion set aside his own ritual for the hungry, how much less should man-made rules bind anyone? Legalism is empty of compassion, because only those who see their own sin cling to Christ's mercy and learn to share it. Third, Jesus rules. As the Son of Man and Lord of the Sabbath, greater than the temple, he owns the day and declares it a day of mercy. He is Lord over our time, rest, money and convictions, so believers are urged to own their sin and replace condemnation with compassion.
30120:
Concluding a series on Jesus' five conflicts with the scribes and Pharisees in Luke, this sermon studies the healing of the man with the withered right hand in Luke 6:6-11. Since Genesis 3:15 the seed of the serpent has fought the seed of the woman, and here self-righteousness meets grace head on. First, the merciful Jesus rules by compassion. The Sabbath was meant to display God's mercy, yet the religious leaders watched Jesus closely, certain of his power and compassion, waiting to accuse him. Knowing their thoughts, Jesus boldly called the man to stand in the middle of the synagogue, refusing to withhold good from the suffering just to avoid offending the self-righteous.

Second, the merciful Jesus exposes self-righteousness. His question, whether it is lawful to do good or harm on the Sabbath, revealed men who examined others' withered hands while blind to their own withered hearts. Their silence grieved and angered him, and across the five conflicts their hearts hardened from questioning, to grumbling, to accusation, to plotting murder. Third, the merciful Jesus does good while his enemies rage: at his word the hand was restored, yet they left filled with fury. Listeners are warned that a decent religious life can still grieve Christ if it refuses correction, and are urged to ask God to burn out their self-righteousness and change them.
30121:
Beginning a new series on the twelve apostles from Luke 6:12-16, this sermon speaks to believers who see their weaknesses clearly and wonder how God could ever use them. God loves to accomplish the impossible through the weak, as Christ's own life shows: he died rejected and poor, yet he is the centre of all history. Before turning to the apostles, Luke fixes our eyes on Jesus as the real secret behind their accomplishment. First, Jesus is mighty in prayer. As hostility rose against him, he did not worry or escape but spent the whole night with his Father, depending on him for the choice of the Twelve and interceding for men who could not even stay awake to pray. He still intercedes for his people today.

Second, Jesus is mighty in choosing. From a great multitude of disciples he sovereignly called just twelve. As with Gideon's three hundred, God uses few so that the glory is plainly his. Third, Jesus is mighty in sending. Apostles are sent out to preach, and that purpose passes to the church. The list itself is striking: no scholars or generals, but fishermen, a zealot, a tax collector and a future traitor. The future of the gospel never rested on these men but on Christ's power, and with Paul believers can boast in their weaknesses.
30124:
Continuing in 1 Peter, this sermon works through 3:13-16, where Peter teaches believers how to respond to persecution and to the trials of life. "Who is there to harm you?" echoes Psalm 34: the Lord does not remove every affliction, but he is near the brokenhearted, and nothing touches his people unless he wills it. As Joseph's story and the cross show, God is sovereign even over the evil intentions of men. Those who suffer for righteousness are blessed, while suffering for doing wrong brings discipline, not reward. In hardship Satan whispers that God has abandoned us, so believers must stand on the written Word rather than their feelings, refusing to fear intimidation.

Instead of fearing, Christians are to sanctify Christ as Lord in their hearts, setting him apart through his Word, surrendering every circumstance to his lordship and drawing strength from him. From that place they must always be ready to defend the hope within them. The sermon corrects the idea that believers should speak only when asked: Peter's readers were questioned because they were already proclaiming Christ and living it. This defence is not for a few online debaters but for the whole church, and it must be made with gentleness, reverence and a clear conscience, aiming to win souls rather than arguments. Unbelievers are urged to trust Christ.
30125:
Introducing a new series on the twelve apostles from Luke 6:13, this sermon removes the marble-statue image of the apostles as superhuman saints. Like Elijah, they were men with a nature like ours. As a group they suffered from "big head disease", arguing over who was greatest even as Jesus spoke of his death. They had "turtle disease", repeatedly failing to understand his plain teaching, and "chicken disease", panicking in the storm and fleeing at his arrest. They were also controlling, turning away children and rebuking a man who cast out demons in Jesus' name. Yet Christ never gave up on them. He washed their feet, patiently taught and corrected them, calmed their fears and met them after the resurrection with "Peace be to you."

Through Christ, these ordinary men carried the gospel across the world, planted churches, wrote Scripture and joyfully suffered martyrdom. God delights to use the weak and despised (2 Corinthians 12:9; 1 Corinthians 1:26-28), so weakness is no barrier to being used by him. What set the apostles apart, Judas excepted, was that they were available and teachable: they left possessions, relationships and businesses to follow Jesus without excuses, and they listened eagerly and asked him to explain. Believers are urged to distinguish immaturity from lack of commitment and to yield themselves fully to Christ.
30130:
Opening the detailed studies in the series on the twelve apostles, this sermon looks at Andrew, the quiet fisherman usually known simply as Simon Peter's brother. He wrote no book, preached no recorded sermon and performed no recorded miracle, yet Christ used him mightily. His life shows what it means to be teachable and available. He was teachable because he hungered for the Word: he travelled long distances to hear John the Baptist's uncompromising preaching rather than settle for comfortable teaching, pressed Jesus privately for deeper understanding, and let hard truth change him. He was available because he hungered for the God of the Word. When John declared "Behold, the Lamb of God" (John 1:35-39), Andrew immediately followed Jesus and asked where he was staying, resolved from his first day to live his life around Christ.

The result was impact, for his eyes were always scanning for souls. The first thing he did was find his brother and bring him to Jesus (John 1:41-42), and that brother became the leader of the apostles. Later he brought seeking Greeks to Christ (John 12:20-22) and pointed to a boy's small lunch before the feeding of the five thousand, trusting Christ's power rather than human resources. Believers are urged to be faithful signposts to Jesus, serving gladly out of the spotlight with whatever little they have.
30131:
Continuing the series on the twelve apostles, this sermon looks at Philip, a cautious, detailed, by-the-book man whose security rested in his own intellect rather than in Christ. Philip is not the hero of the story but a window onto the patience and sufficiency of the Saviour, seen at three points in his life. In John 1:43-45 Jesus finds Philip and calls him to follow, and Philip tells Nathanael that he has found the Messiah. Yet salvation always begins with God: no one seeks him unless the Father draws them (Romans 3; John 6:44), so believers should be deeply grateful and the unconverted should cry out to Christ now. In John 6, Jesus tests Philip before feeding the five thousand. Philip runs the numbers and concludes it is impossible, overlooking the all-powerful Lord standing beside him.

In John 14:8-10, after three years with Jesus, Philip asks to be shown the Father, as though Christ were not enough. Jesus patiently answers that whoever has seen him has seen the Father. Philip had studied the signposts without beholding the one they pointed to. Christians are warned that they can know much about Jesus yet think too little of him, and that ministry at church or at home without his strength is death. Ordinary people who stay teachable and available can be mightily used by Christ.
30132:
Preached for weary saints facing pressures and trials, this sermon on John 21:1-14, "Breakfast on the Beach", shows the risen Christ revealing himself to his disciples in two comforting ways. First, he is our provision. Seven disciples, Peter among them still carrying his denial, have returned to Galilee in obedience to Jesus' command, yet they fish all night and catch nothing. Obedience does not remove hardship, but Jesus stands on the shore watching over them and calls them "children", his little ones. At his word the net fills with 153 large fish. Without him there is emptiness; with him there is satisfaction. As Creator he provides every meal and every breath, and even trials are part of his providence, weaning his people from the world. Peter throws himself into the sea, wanting Jesus more than the fish.

Second, Jesus is our compassion. He has already prepared a charcoal fire with fish and bread, and he serves the weary men breakfast with his own hands, just as he once washed their feet. The sermon closes with a long reading of New Testament commands, the obedience God blesses as a way of living once saved, in the Spirit's power. Christians are urged to long for Jesus more than his gifts and to keep going even when the net is empty.
30133:
Continuing the series on the twelve apostles, this sermon studies Nathanael, also called Bartholomew, from John 1:43-51. The whole series rests on one encouragement: if Christ chose and changed such ordinary, flawed men, he can use anyone who is available and teachable. When Philip announces that he has found the one Moses and the prophets wrote about, Nathanael scoffs, "Can any good thing come out of Nazareth?" He let outward appearances shape his view of Christ, missing that the Messiah's humble origins were part of his greatness, the same humility that led him to the cross. Believers are warned not to let trials, sickness or unanswered prayer build a wall that hides the greatness of Christ.

Philip simply says, "Come and see", and Jesus greets Nathanael as an Israelite in whom there is no deceit: not a sinless man, but one who did not hide or excuse his sin as the self-righteous leaders did. Jesus' knowledge of him under the fig tree shows that Christ knows every secret of the heart, and the sermon draws comfort from this, since he knows his people's worst and still loves them. Nathanael confesses him as Rabbi, Son of God and King of Israel, and Jesus promises he will see greater things. With Paul in Philippians 3, listeners are urged to press on to know Christ.
30134:
Continuing the series on the twelve apostles, this sermon turns to two of the least known, James the son of Alphaeus and Thaddeus. The Twelve appear in three groups of four, and these men belong to the last, the group the Gospels say least about. Their names do them no favours: Thaddeus can be read as "mama's boy" and James is called "the less", the little or least important one. Yet they were teachable and available, and when Peter said "we have left everything and followed you" in Mark 10, they stood among those for whom Christ was worth more than anything they had left behind. They represent the unknown army of the Lord: the prayer warriors, the faithful servants and the quiet workers through whom the church actually grows.

Mark 10:35-45 then shows what greatness means in God's kingdom. James and John sought the top positions, but Jesus taught that greatness is found not in rank, gifts or fame but in becoming a servant, even a slave, of all the brethren, following the Son of Man who came to serve and give his life as a ransom for many. Believers are urged to pray "use me" and let the Lord choose how, to serve without seeking applause, and to keep returning to Christ for strength so they do not burn out.
30136:
Opening a study of 1 Peter 3:18-22, often called one of the hardest passages in the Bible, this sermon focuses on verse 18 alone: Christ died for sins once for all, the just for the unjust, to bring us to God. Peter is writing to a persecuted church, and he reminds them that Christ also suffered. Jesus was no murderer, thief or blasphemer, yet he bore the wrath of God in his own body, so no believer's suffering will ever compare with his. Every death is deserved because all have sinned, but his alone was unjust, planned by God and purposeful. Because he offered himself once for all, his sacrifice covers past, present and future sins, and salvation is Christ alone, not Christ plus church attendance, Bible reading or good works.

The just died for the unjust, and Scripture's record of Moses, Paul, Rahab, David, the thief on the cross and Peter shows that no sinner is beyond his reach. He does more than make salvation available: he personally brings his people to God. Believers are called to remember that suffering for God's glory is never wasted, to stop deciding who might be saved, and to love the unlovable and keep proclaiming the gospel. The unconverted are urged to come to Christ for rest now.
30137:
Continuing in 1 Peter 3, this sermon works through one of the most debated passages in the New Testament, verses 19 to 22, to show that Christ is victorious over every power. Peter wrote to believers under persecution, and behind that hostility stands an enemy who has opposed God since the fall. Weighing several interpretations, the sermon concludes that after his death Christ went and proclaimed his triumph, not a second chance of salvation, to imprisoned fallen angels who sinned in the days of Noah, linking the passage with Genesis 6, 2 Peter 2 and Jude. Their rebellion and the corruption of that age resemble the sexual sin and spiritual darkness of our own culture.

God showed great patience while Noah preached and built the ark, yet only eight people were saved. Peter presents Christ as the better ark: he bore the judgment, carries his people through it and, raised and ascended, now reigns with angels and powers subject to him. Believers are encouraged that Satan can do nothing beyond God's permission, and that they should keep proclaiming the gospel patiently even when few respond and many mock. The sermon closes with an urgent appeal to come to Christ now, because God's patience will not wait forever and the door of the ark will one day be shut.
30139:
Thomas has long carried the label "doubting Thomas," but this sermon argues that doubt was not his defining trait, since all the disciples struggled to believe in the resurrection. What stands out in the Gospel of John is a pessimistic temperament. When Jesus resolved to return to Judea to raise Lazarus, Thomas expected only death, and on the night before the cross he answered the promise of a prepared place with "we do not know the way." Negativity drains joy, breeds self-preservation and gives Christ the bare minimum. The remedy is not mere positive thinking but filling the mind with what is excellent and praiseworthy, above all Christ himself.

Yet Thomas also showed real courage. Bravery is not the absence of fear but following Christ when every part of you is afraid, as Jesus did in Gethsemane, and Thomas urged the others to go and die with their Master. Grieving deeply after the crucifixion, he refused to believe the reports of the resurrection. Jesus came to him with peace, offered his wounds and called him to believe. Thomas responded with the highest confession in the Gospels, "My Lord and my God." Because Christ is risen, the payment for sin is accepted, death is defeated and believers will rise to enjoy him forever.
30143:
Continuing the series on the twelve apostles, this sermon traces how the grace of God transformed John, the young fisherman Jesus named a Son of Thunder. John was likely a teenager when he began following Christ, and he came from a devoted family. His mother Salome followed Jesus from Galilee to Jerusalem, supported his ministry, stood at the cross and went early to the tomb. His father Zebedee released his sons and wife to follow Christ at real cost to himself. Their example challenges parents to treasure Christ above comfort, wealth or success and to give their children Christ, and calls young people to be wholehearted for Jesus while they are young.

Yet John badly needed grace. Soon after seeing Christ's glory on the mountain he argued over who was greatest, tried to stop a man casting out demons in Jesus' name, and wanted to call fire down on a Samaritan village. Jesus patiently corrected him and then showed him love at the cross, where he forgave his enemies and entrusted his mother to John's care. That grace remade John into the apostle of love, who later preached to the Samaritans and wrote that believers ought to lay down their lives for one another. The sermon calls listeners with anger, control or impatience to be teachable and available, because grace does not only forgive but continues to change.
